items.status: FIXED — filed and closed 2026-10-10 by lang-50 (Order 50), commit aa573089 on branch lang-50
items.title: A directed array literal at an OPEN element left the element unbound natively — `first(["a", "b", "c"])` against `fun first<T>(values: [T; 3])`, and `Trio { slots = [7, 8, 9] }` for `struct Trio<T> { slots: [T; 3] }`, were refused natively "does not emit a value of an unbound generic type parameter" while JS printed the answer
items.body: Pre-existing on v0.47.0. infer_type_inner's directed array-literal arm answered with the constraint's element id, so the call reconciled the callee's `T` with itself. Now the literal types its element by its items wherever the expected element is open (a grounded one keeps the constraint's id, so nothing that compiled natively moves).

items.title: A subtrait impl over a STRUCTURAL subject (a tuple or a fixed array) cannot reach its supertrait's impl through an element's sub-bound — `impl (type A: Louder, type B: Louder) with Loud {}` (with `trait Loud with Shown`, `trait Louder with Display` and `impl (type A: Display, type B: Display) with Shown`) is refused "'(A, B)' does not implement trait 'Loud': missing 'shown'"; the nominal twin (`impl Box2<type T: Eq> with Eq {}` over `impl Box2<type T: PartialEq> with PartialEq`) compiles
items.body: Pre-existing on v0.47.0 for tuples; array-lengths S5 met it as `impl [type T: Eq; _] with Eq {}` beside std's new `impl [type T: PartialEq; const N] with PartialEq`, so arrays (and tuples) ship without `Eq`. The conformance walk that looks for the supertrait member on the subtrait impl's subject finds the supertrait impl for a nominal subject whose binder's bound implies the supertrait impl's element bound (Eq => PartialEq), and does not for a tuple/array subject. Expected: compiles, and `fun needs<T: Eq>(v: T)` accepts a `[i32; 2]` once std writes the impl. Sizing S; the supertrait-member search in conformance.

items.title: Natively the INNER literals of a nested array literal handed to a callee whose parameter is generic over its own binders emit as `Vec`s — `grid == [[1, 2], [3, 4]]` (std's `impl [type T: PartialEq; const N]`, whose `b: [T; N]` is the argument's expected type, unsubstituted) is refused by rustc "expected `[i32; 2]`, found `Vec<i32>`"; JS prints `true`
items.body: The analyzer types the operand by the left side (a wrong inner count is refused "this array literal has 3 elements, but its type is `[_; 2]`"), but records no type for the nested literals, so the native list-literal arm falls back to the expected type, the callee's `[T; N]`: the outer literal now takes its own count (array-lengths S5), and the inner one meets `T`, which resolves to nothing under the caller's substitution, and renders `vec![..]`. Fix: the argument's expected type under the CALL's substitution (T = [i32; 2], N = 2), or the analyzer recording a directed literal's settled type. A flat literal (`fixed == [1, 2, 3]`) builds. Sizing S; vilan-rust's call-argument expectation.

items.title: An `[rpc]` parameter of fixed-array type is refused twice for one cause, and the second refusal names the type `_` — "in code generated by this attribute: [u8; 4] has no method 'describe'" and "parameter `rgba` of `[rpc]` method `first` is `_`, which is not Wire"
items.body: Read while checking array-lengths.md §3's claim that an rpc signature holding `[u8; 4]` keeps its contract hash: no contract can hold an array today (an array is not Wire), so that pin is not writable. The Wire refusal renders the parameter's type through a printer that answers `_` for an array, and the service derive's generated code fails first on `describe`. Expected: one refusal, naming `[u8; 4]`. Whether arrays should be Wire (`impl [type T: Wire; const N] with Wire`, now writable) is the owner's call (the paper's Q13 deferred it). Sizing S.

items.title: `vilan run` of the INSTALLED toolchain reads std from the nearest vilan checkout when the program sits inside one — a probe under `vilan/.claude/worktrees/lang-50/target/` ran v0.47.0 against the worktree's edited std ("found '[' expected a type" at the new `impl [type T: PartialEq; const N]`), and a debug build reads `crates/vilan-cli/../../vilan/std` at run time, so editing std mid-suite poisons a running `nextest`
items.body: Two effects a lane can trip over: (1) a 'base compiler' probe written inside a checkout is not a base probe; (2) std edits during a running suite change the std every subsequently spawned compile reads (the corpus and native legs all failed for one in-flight std edit). Neither is necessarily wrong — a dev build reading the tree's std is the point — but the lane mechanics should say so (probes for the base run from the scratchpad, outside any checkout; no std or docs edits while a suite runs). Sizing XS (docs: AGENTS.md / the Mechanics).
